For the Muslim corps member who finds themselves as the only Muslim or the only moral voice in a morally compromised environment: Lut's story shows that standing alone for righteousness, even when it costs you everything, is honored by Allah above all social belonging.
sunday.source: Quran 29:26-35; Quran 11:77-83; Tafsir Ibn Kathir, Surah al-Ankabut; Stories of the Prophets by Ibn Kathir

monday.title: Hadith on the Importance of Fajr Prayer
monday.arabic_text: مَنْ صَلَّى الصُّبْحَ فَهُوَ فِي ذِمَّةِ اللَّهِ
monday.english_text: Whoever prays Fajr is under the protection of Allah.
monday.reported_by: Narrated by Jundab ibn Abdullah (may Allah be pleased with him). Recorded in Sahih Muslim (657).
monday.lesson: Fajr prayer is the most rewarded and the most difficult. Praying Fajr in congregation is described as better than the world and everything in it (Jami' al-Tirmidhi 3390). Those who pray Fajr and Isha in congregation are counted as having prayed the whole night. For a corps member, establishing Fajr sets the tone for the entire day — spiritually and practically.
monday.source: Sahih Muslim, Hadith 657; Jami' al-Tirmidhi, Hadith 3390; Riyad as-Salihin, Chapter on Fajr Prayer

monday.title: Hadith on Brotherhood
monday.arabic_text: الْمُسْلِمُ أَخُو الْمُسْلِمِ، لَا يَظْلِمُهُ وَلَا يُسْلِمُهُ
monday.english_text: A Muslim is the brother of a Muslim: he does not wrong him, and he does not abandon him.
monday.transliteration: Al-muslmu akhu-l-muslim, la yadhlimhu wa la yuslimuhu.
monday.chain_of_narration: Abdullah ibn Umar (RA) → Nafi' → Malik ibn Anas
monday.reported_by: Narrated by Abdullah ibn Umar (may Allah be pleased with him). Recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari (2442) and Sahih Muslim (2580).
monday.lesson: Islamic brotherhood has two components: protection from harm AND active support in need. Not abandoning a Muslim in need is as obligatory as not harming them. For corps members: when a Muslim colleague is being mistreated, slandered, or is struggling — remaining silent is itself a form of abandonment. Stand by your brother or sister — not through injustice, but through honest support.
monday.source: Sahih al-Bukhari, Hadith 2442; Sahih Muslim, Hadith 2580; Riyad as-Salihin, Chapter on Brotherhood

tuesday.title: The Three Quls — Protective Surahs Before Sleep
tuesday.arabic_text: قُلْ هُوَ اللَّهُ أَحَدٌ... قُلْ أَعُوذُ بِرَبِّ الْفَلَقِ... قُلْ أَعُوذُ بِرَبِّ النَّاسِ
tuesday.english_text: Say: He is Allah, One... Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of daybreak... Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind.
tuesday.transliteration: Qul huwa Allahu ahad... Qul a'udhu bi-Rabbil-falaq... Qul a'udhu bi-Rabbin-nas.
tuesday.benefits: The Prophet recited Surah al-Ikhlas, al-Falaq, and an-Nas (the three Quls) together after each of the five daily prayers, and three times each before sleeping — blowing into his cupped hands and wiping over his body. These surahs together affirm pure Tawheed (al-Ikhlas), seek protection from external evil (al-Falaq), and seek protection from internal whispers and social evil (an-Nas). A daily practice every corps member should establish.
tuesday.source: Sahih al-Bukhari, Hadith 5017; Sunan Abi Dawud, Hadith 5056; Hisn al-Muslim by Sa'id al-Qahtani

tuesday.title: Du'a for Protection from the Evil Eye
tuesday.arabic_text: أَعُوذُ بِكَلِمَاتِ اللَّهِ التَّامَّاتِ مِنْ شَرِّ مَا خَلَقَ
tuesday.english_text: I seek refuge in the perfect words of Allah from the evil of what He has created.
tuesday.transliteration: A'udhu bikalimati-llahit-tammati min sharri ma khalaq.
tuesday.benefits: The Prophet said: 'Whoever says this when evening comes, no harm from that night will touch him.' (Sahih Muslim 2709). The evil eye (al-'ayn) is real — the Prophet affirmed it and provided this protection. For corps members in new communities where jealousy or envy may exist, and especially when receiving praise or compliments — seek protection with these words. Add: 'La ilaha illallah' and 'Bismillah' to any blessing you receive.
tuesday.source: Sahih Muslim, Hadith 2709; Jami' al-Tirmidhi, Hadith 3437; Hisn al-Muslim by Sa'id al-Qahtani

wednesday.title: Ihsan — The Third Level of Religion
wednesday.arabic_text: الإِحْسَانُ أَنْ تَعْبُدَ اللَّهَ كَأَنَّكَ تَرَاهُ، فَإِنْ لَمْ تَكُنْ تَرَاهُ فَإِنَّهُ يَرَاكَ
wednesday.english_text: Ihsan is to worship Allah as if you see Him; and although you cannot see Him, He sees you.
wednesday.lesson:
The Hadith of Jibril establishes three levels of the religion: Islam (outward submission), Iman (inward belief), and Ihsan (excellence of worship). Ihsan is the highest level — it means performing every act of worship as though you are in Allah's direct presence. A person of Ihsan prays not to be seen by others, gives charity not for reputation, and works not to impress supervisors — but because Allah is watching.

For a Muslim corps member: Ihsan transforms every moment of service year into sustained excellence. It means your report is accurate whether or not the inspector checks it, your duties are fulfilled whether or not your supervisor is present, your character is consistent in private and in public.
wednesday.extra_notes:
Q: How do I develop Ihsan?
A: The scholars list several means: consistent voluntary worship (nafl prayers, fasting, dhikr), reading about Allah's greatness (Asma and Sifat), maintaining wudu throughout the day, recalling death frequently, and spending time with the righteous. Ihsan is a state of the heart achieved through sustained spiritual practice.
wednesday.source: Sahih Muslim, Hadith 8 (Hadith of Jibril); Madarij as-Salikin by Ibn al-Qayyim; Al-Risalah al-Qushayriyyah by al-Qushayri

wednesday.title: Al-Muraqabah — Awareness of Allah's Watching
wednesday.english_text: And He is with you wherever you are. (Quran 57:4)
wednesday.lesson:
Al-Muraqabah (watchful awareness of Allah) is the practical state of Ihsan. It means living with the consciousness that Allah is always present — not as a physical presence in a location, but in His knowledge and awareness of everything. The believer in muraqabah never needs external supervision because Allah's supervision is constant.

For corps members: Your character in your bedroom, in your private phone conversations, in your innermost thoughts — Allah is aware of all of it. This is not a frightening statement for the sincere Muslim — it is a liberating one. You need not perform for anyone, because the only audience that ultimately matters is already watching.
wednesday.extra_notes: Real-life scenario: A corps member is alone with their PPA's financial records and discovers money has been mismanaged. No one else knows they found out. The person of muraqabah reports it regardless — because they live for Allah's approval, not human approval.
wednesday.source: Tafsir Ibn Kathir, Quran 57:4; Madarij as-Salikin by Ibn al-Qayyim; Al-Aqeedah al-Wasitiyyah by Ibn Taymiyyah

thursday.title: Fiqh of Hajj — The Fifth Pillar
thursday.arabic_text: وَلِلَّهِ عَلَى النَّاسِ حِجُّ الْبَيْتِ مَنِ اسْتَطَاعَ إِلَيْهِ سَبِيلًا
thursday.english_text: And pilgrimage to the House is a duty for people upon whomever is able to find a way. (Quran 3:97)
thursday.lesson:
Hajj is the fifth pillar of Islam — obligatory once in a lifetime for the Muslim who is physically able and financially capable (having expenses for the journey and the ability to leave provision for their dependents). The pillars of Hajj include: Ihram, standing at Arafah (the essential pillar), Tawaf al-Ifadah, and Sa'y between Safa and Marwa.

For corps members: Most will not yet have performed Hajj. Begin planning and saving. The Prophet said: 'Hasten to perform Hajj, for none of you knows what will befall him.' (Musnad Ahmad). As a young person with health and time, make Hajj a priority in the years following your service.
thursday.extra_notes:
Difference between Hajj and Umrah:
- Umrah: can be performed at any time, shorter rites (Ihram, Tawaf, Sa'y, shaving/cutting hair), highly recommended but not obligatory for most
- Hajj: specific days in Dhul-Hijjah, includes Arafah, Muzdalifah, Mina, stoning of Jamarat, and sacrifice

For those who cannot perform Hajj this year: Fast the Day of Arafah (Dhul-Hijjah 9) — the Prophet said it expiates sins of the previous and coming year (Sahih Muslim 1162).
thursday.source: Fiqh us-Sunnah by Sayyid Sabiq, Vol. 5; Al-Fiqh al-Islami wa Adillatuh by Wahbah az-Zuhayli; Al-Mughni by Ibn Qudamah

thursday.title: Fiqh of Udhiyah — The Sacrifice of Eid al-Adha
thursday.arabic_text: فَصَلِّ لِرَبِّكَ وَانْحَرْ
thursday.english_text: So pray to your Lord and sacrifice. (Quran 108:2)
thursday.lesson:
Udhiyah (sacrifice on Eid al-Adha) is Sunnah Mu'akkadah (strongly emphasized Sunnah) according to the majority, and wajib (obligatory) according to the Hanafi school for those with sufficient means. It commemorates Ibrahim (AS)'s willingness to sacrifice his son. The sacrifice is permissible for: a sheep or goat (for one person), a cow or buffalo (for up to seven people), or a camel (for up to seven people).

For corps members: If your allowance savings allow it, participating in a group udhiyah (splitting the cost of a cow with six others) is the economically accessible way to fulfill this Sunnah during your service year.
thursday.extra_notes:
Q: Can I send money home for the family's udhiyah to be done on my behalf?
A: Yes. The head of the household can perform udhiyah on behalf of the entire family. Sending money home for your parents to sacrifice on behalf of the family is fully valid.

Note on the meat: The Sunnah is to divide the sacrifice into thirds: one third for yourself and family, one third as gifts to relatives and friends, one third as sadaqah to the poor.
thursday.source: Al-Fiqh al-Islami wa Adillatuh by Wahbah az-Zuhayli; Fiqh us-Sunnah by Sayyid Sabiq; Al-Mughni by Ibn Qudamah

friday.title: The Khutbah — Content, Length, and Impact
friday.arabic_text: إِنَّ طُولَ صَلَاةِ الرَّجُلِ وَقِصَرَ خُطْبَتِهِ مَئِنَّةٌ مِنْ فِقْهِهِ
friday.english_text: A man's lengthening of his prayer and shortening of his sermon is a sign of his understanding (fiqh).
friday.lesson:
The Prophet's guidance on the Jumu'ah khutbah is that it should be concise, impactful, and practically applicable. A long, meandering khutbah that puts people to sleep violates the Sunnah. The ideal: begin with hamd and salawat, deliver two clear points with Quranic and Hadith evidence, and end with du'a — all within 20-30 minutes.

For Muslim corps members who serve as amir or Islamic officer for their group: if you are called to deliver a khutbah, prepare well. Your khutbah should speak to the real challenges of your community — not be disconnected from their lived reality.
friday.extra_notes:
Structure of a valid Jumu'ah khutbah:
1. First khutbah: Hamd, Shahada, Salawat, taqwa reminder, Quranic verse(s), main content
2. Brief sitting between khutbahs
3. Second khutbah: Hamd, Salawat, shorter reminder, du'a for Muslims
4. Begin Salah with iqamah
friday.source: Sahih Muslim, Hadith 869; Fiqh us-Sunnah by Sayyid Sabiq; Al-Mughni by Ibn Qudamah

friday.title: Friday Azkar — Istikhara Before the Week
friday.arabic_text: اللَّهُمَّ خِرْ لِي وَاخْتَرْ لِي
friday.english_text: O Allah, choose what is good for me and make that choice for me.
friday.transliteration: Allahumma khir li wakhtar li.
friday.benefits: Friday is the ideal day to make du'a and perform Istikhara for the decisions facing you in the coming week. After Jumu'ah prayer, in the remaining hours before Maghrib, make this concise du'a and the full Istikhara supplication from Sahih al-Bukhari for any decision weighing on your heart — a job choice, a relationship decision, a project direction. Trust Allah to guide the path.
friday.source: Masnun du'a related to Istikhara; al-Adhkar by Imam an-Nawawi; Hisn al-Muslim by Sa'id al-Qahtani

saturday.title: Az-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam (RA) — The Disciple of the Prophet
saturday.arabic_text: إِنَّ لِكُلِّ نَبِيٍّ حَوَارِيًّا وَحَوَارِيِّي الزُّبَيْرُ
saturday.english_text: Every prophet has a disciple and my disciple is az-Zubayr.
saturday.lesson:
Az-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam was the first person to draw a sword in the way of Allah — at the age of twelve, after hearing a false rumor that the Prophet had been captured. He was the cousin of the Prophet (his mother Safiyyah was the Prophet's aunt), married to Asma bint Abi Bakr, and was described by the Prophet as his most trusted confidant.

At the Battle of Badr, Uhud, Khandaq, and Hudaybiyyah — az-Zubayr was always at the forefront. He was known for his physical courage, his loyalty, and his willingness to sacrifice everything for his faith.

Lesson: Real loyalty is demonstrated in difficult moments, not easy ones. The Muslim corps member who stands by their principles when it is costly — in their workplace, their community, their relationships — is demonstrating something of az-Zubayr's character.
saturday.source: Sahih al-Bukhari, Hadith 2846; Jami' al-Tirmidhi, Hadith 3745; Siyar A'lam an-Nubala by Imam adh-Dhahabi

saturday.title: Asma bint Abi Bakr (RA) — Dhatu-n-Nitaqayn (The One of Two Belts)
saturday.arabic_text: لَا تُوعِي فَيُوعِيَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْكِ
saturday.english_text: Do not hoard, so that Allah does not withhold from you.
saturday.lesson:
Asma bint Abi Bakr (RA) was called 'Dhatu-n-Nitaqayn' (she of two belts) because she tore her own belt in two to tie the food provisions for the Prophet and her father Abu Bakr during the Hijrah — a moment of extraordinary sacrifice and courage. When her son Abdullah ibn az-Zubayr was killed and crucified by the Umayyad forces, she went to see his body, composed and firm, at nearly 100 years old.

Throughout her life she was known for extraordinary generosity — she gave away everything she earned and never stored anything, trusting Allah completely.

Lesson: The strength of a Muslim woman of faith does not waver even in the most devastating personal loss. Asma's composure before the body of her son is one of the most moving examples of Iman in the face of trial in Islamic history.
saturday.source: Sahih al-Bukhari, Hadith 2979; Al-Isabah fi Tamyiz as-Sahabah by Ibn Hajar; Siyar A'lam an-Nubala by Imam adh-Dhahabi

sunday.title: The Hypocrites (Munafiqun) — The Internal Threat
sunday.arabic_text: إِنَّ الْمُنَافِقِينَ فِي الدَّرْكِ الْأَسْفَلِ مِنَ النَّارِ
sunday.english_text: Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest depths of the Fire. (Quran 4:145)
sunday.lesson:
The munafiqun (hypocrites) of Madinah appeared as Muslims but acted against Islam internally. The Quran dedicates an entire surah (al-Munafiqun) and extensive passages of Surah al-Baqarah and an-Nisa to warning against their traits: they lie, break promises, betray trust, are lazy in worship, show off when praying, mock the believers privately, and ally with the enemies of Islam.

For the corps member: The Prophet identified four signs of the hypocrite: when he speaks, he lies; when he makes a promise, he breaks it; when he is trusted, he betrays it; when he disputes, he behaves wickedly (Sahih al-Bukhari 33). Self-examine regularly — these traits can exist in a Muslim's character as isolated moral failings, and must be corrected.
sunday.source: Quran 63:1-11; Quran 2:8-20; Tafsir Ibn Kathir, Surah al-Munafiqun; Sahih al-Bukhari, Hadith 33

sunday.title: The Slander of Aisha (RA) — Patience and Divine Vindication
sunday.arabic_text: إِنَّ الَّذِينَ جَاءُوا بِالْإِفْكِ عُصْبَةٌ مِّنكُمْ
sunday.english_text: Indeed, those who came with the slander are a group among you. (Quran 24:11)
sunday.lesson:
When Aisha (RA) was falsely accused of immorality by the munafiqun, it caused enormous pain to her, the Prophet, and the Muslim community for an entire month. The Prophet did not immediately dismiss or confirm the accusation. Finally, Allah revealed ten verses of Surah an-Nur declaring her innocence — verses that will be recited until the Day of Judgment.

The response of Aisha's parents, Abu Bakr and Umm Ruman: full support for their daughter. The response of Abu Bakr to the Quranic revelation: increased charity to the companion who had spread the slander.

Lesson: False accusation is a great wrong with Quranic-level consequences. Guard your tongue. And when falsely accused yourself, follow Aisha's path: patience, prayer, and trust that Allah's justice will come.
sunday.source: Quran 24:11-26; Sahih al-Bukhari, Hadith 4141 (Aisha's own account); Tafsir Ibn Kathir, Surah an-Nur

monday.title: Hadith on Excellence in Work
monday.arabic_text: إِنَّ اللَّهَ يُحِبُّ إِذَا عَمِلَ أَحَدُكُمْ عَمَلًا أَنْ يُتْقِنَهُ
monday.english_text: Indeed, Allah loves it when one of you performs a deed to do it with excellence (itqan).
monday.transliteration: Innallaha yuhibbu idha 'amila ahadukum 'amalan an yutqinahu.
monday.reported_by: Narrated by Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her). Recorded in al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman and authenticated by al-Albani.
monday.lesson: Itqan means doing something with the highest possible excellence — not just completing it, but perfecting it. This hadith makes professional excellence a form of worship. Whether you are teaching in a school, working in a hospital, coding in a tech company, or organizing community projects — doing it with itqan is what Allah loves. Mediocrity in work when you are capable of better is, in a sense, a spiritual failure.
monday.source: Al-Bayhaqi, Shu'ab al-Iman; Authenticated by al-Albani in Silsilah as-Sahihah (1113); Mawsu'at al-Akhlaq by Khalid al-Sabt

monday.title: Hadith on the Virtues of Dhikr
monday.arabic_text: أَلَا أُنَبِّئُكُمْ بِخَيْرِ أَعْمَالِكُمْ وَأَزْكَاهَا عِنْدَ مَلِيكِكُمْ وَأَرْفَعِهَا فِي دَرَجَاتِكُمْ؟ ذِكْرُ اللَّهِ
monday.english_text: Shall I not tell you of the best of your deeds and the purest in the sight of your King, and the highest in raising your degrees? Dhikr of Allah.
monday.transliteration: Ala unabbi'ukum bikhayri a'malikum wa azkaha 'inda maleekikum wa arfa'iha fi darajatikum? Dhikarullahi.
monday.chain_of_narration: Abu Darda' (RA) → Makhul → narrated in Muwatta and others
monday.reported_by: Narrated by Abu Darda' (may Allah be pleased with him). Recorded in Jami' al-Tirmidhi (3377) and al-Muwatta of Imam Malik, classified as Sahih.
monday.lesson: Among all deeds, dhikr of Allah is declared the best and most elevating. Better than giving sadaqah, better than fighting in battle — this is what the Prophet declared. Yet dhikr costs nothing, requires no specific location, and can be done in any moment of the day. The Muslim corps member who maintains constant dhikr throughout their working day is performing the best deed available to them — continuously.
monday.source: Jami' al-Tirmidhi, Hadith 3377; Al-Muwatta of Imam Malik; Riyad as-Salihin, Chapter on Dhikr

tuesday.title: Du'a for Entering a New Town or City
tuesday.arabic_text: اللَّهُمَّ رَبَّ السَّمَاوَاتِ السَّبْعِ وَمَا أَظْلَلْنَ، وَرَبَّ الْأَرَضِينَ السَّبْعِ وَمَا أَقْلَلْنَ، وَرَبَّ الشَّيَاطِينِ وَمَا أَضْلَلْنَ، وَرَبَّ الرِّيَاحِ وَمَا أَذْرَيْنَ، فَإِنِّي أَسْأَلُكَ خَيْرَ هَذِهِ الْقَرْيَةِ وَخَيْرَ أَهْلِهَا، وَأَعُوذُ بِكَ مِنْ شَرِّهَا وَشَرِّ أَهْلِهَا
tuesday.english_text: O Allah, Lord of the seven heavens and all they overshadow, Lord of the seven earths and all they carry, Lord of the shayateen and all they lead astray, and Lord of the winds and all they scatter — I ask You for the good of this town and the good of its people, and I seek refuge in You from its evil and the evil of its people.
tuesday.transliteration: Allahumma Rabbas-samawatis-sab'i wa ma azlalna, wa Rabbal-aradinas-sab'i wa ma aqulalna...
tuesday.benefits: This is the Sunnah du'a when arriving at a new town — narrated by Suhayl ibn Abi Salih from his father. A corps member arriving at their posting location for the first time should stop and recite this du'a. It establishes spiritual ownership over your new environment — seeking its blessings and seeking protection from its harms before you even begin your work.
tuesday.source: Al-Adab al-Mufrad by Imam al-Bukhari, Hadith 1235; Authenticated by al-Albani; Hisn al-Muslim by Sa'id al-Qahtani

tuesday.title: Du'a for Difficult Matters — Allahuma la sahla
tuesday.arabic_text: اللَّهُمَّ لَا سَهْلَ إِلَّا مَا جَعَلْتَهُ سَهْلًا، وَأَنْتَ تَجْعَلُ الْحَزْنَ إِذَا شِئْتَ سَهْلًا
tuesday.english_text: O Allah, nothing is easy except what You make easy, and You make the difficult easy when You will it.
tuesday.transliteration: Allahumma la sahla illa ma ja'altahu sahlan, wa anta taj'alul-hazna idha shi'ta sahlan.
tuesday.benefits: This short du'a is used when facing a difficult task, a challenging conversation, a daunting exam, or any difficult matter. It reminds the believer that ease and difficulty are entirely in Allah's hands — the hardest situation can become simple in an instant by His will. A corps member facing a demanding supervisor, a difficult project, or a complex community problem should recite this before engaging.
tuesday.source: Narrated by Anas ibn Malik (RA) through various chains; Ibn Hibban; Authenticated by al-Albani; Hisn al-Muslim by Sa'id al-Qahtani

wednesday.title: Al-Khashyah — Proper Fear of Allah
wednesday.arabic_text: إِنَّمَا يَخْشَى اللَّهَ مِنْ عِبَادِهِ الْعُلَمَاءُ
wednesday.english_text: Indeed, it is only those who are knowledgeable among His servants who fear Allah. (Quran 35:28)
wednesday.lesson:
Khashyah (awe-inspiring fear of Allah) is different from ordinary fear (khawf). Khashyah is based on knowledge of Allah — the more you know of His power, His attributes, and His justice, the deeper your khashyah becomes. The verse links khashyah directly to 'ulama' (the knowledgeable) — not because only scholars fear Allah, but because proper fear of Allah increases proportionally with knowledge of Him.

A corps member who studies the names and attributes of Allah, the stories of the Quran, the accounts of the Day of Judgment — will naturally develop khashyah that transforms their behavior without any external enforcement.
wednesday.extra_notes:
Q: Is fear the main emotion I should have towards Allah?
A: No. Islamic scholars teach that the believer's heart should contain three things in balance: mahabbah (love), khawf (fear), and raja' (hope). Ibn al-Qayyim compared this to a bird: the body is mahabbah (love), and the two wings are khawf and raja'. A bird flies with both wings — one alone causes crashing.
wednesday.source: Tafsir Ibn Kathir, Quran 35:28; Madarij as-Salikin by Ibn al-Qayyim; Ighathat al-Lahfan by Ibn al-Qayyim

wednesday.title: Ar-Raja' — Hope in Allah's Mercy
wednesday.arabic_text: قُلْ يَا عِبَادِيَ الَّذِينَ أَسْرَفُوا عَلَىٰ أَنفُسِهِمْ لَا تَقْنَطُوا مِن رَّحْمَةِ اللَّهِ
wednesday.english_text: Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah. (Quran 39:53)
wednesday.lesson:
Despair of Allah's mercy (qunoot) is considered a greater sin than many acts of disobedience because it is a statement about Allah — that He is not merciful, or that your sin is greater than His mercy. Both are false. The Prophet said: 'Allah's mercy encompasses all things' (7:156). The famous hadith qudsi says: 'O son of Adam, if your sins were to reach the clouds of the sky and you asked My forgiveness, I would forgive you.' (Jami' al-Tirmidhi 3540).

For corps members who have fallen into sin during their service year: the door of tawbah is always open. No sin is too great for Allah's mercy as long as you are alive.
wednesday.extra_notes:
Q: What about those who committed shirk — is their hope lost?
A: Shirk committed in this life is forgiven with sincere tawbah before death (Quran 39:53-54). The hadith and Quran are clear: the only category that cannot be forgiven is dying upon shirk without tawbah. As long as you are alive and your soul has not reached your throat, tawbah from any sin — including shirk — is accepted.
wednesday.source: Tafsir Ibn Kathir, Quran 39:53; Jami' al-Tirmidhi, Hadith 3540; Madarij as-Salikin by Ibn al-Qayyim

thursday.title: Fiqh of the Night Prayer — Qiyam al-Layl
thursday.arabic_text: تَتَجَافَىٰ جُنُوبُهُمْ عَنِ الْمَضَاجِعِ يَدْعُونَ رَبَّهُمْ خَوْفًا وَطَمَعًا
thursday.english_text: Their sides forsake their beds; they supplicate their Lord in fear and in hope. (Quran 32:16)
thursday.lesson:
Qiyam al-Layl (night prayer) is the highest voluntary prayer in Islam. The Prophet said: 'The best prayer after the obligatory prayers is the night prayer.' (Sahih Muslim 1163). It consists of any number of rak'ahs after Isha until Fajr, ending ideally with Witr (an odd number of rak'ahs). The Sunnah is to pray 8 rak'ahs of Tahajjud plus 3 of Witr.

Benefits: Forgiveness of sins, elevation in status, special closeness to Allah in the last third of the night when Allah descends and says: 'Who is calling on Me that I may respond?'
thursday.extra_notes:
How to establish night prayer:
1. Sleep early after Isha
2. Set an alarm for the last third of the night
3. Begin with two short rak'ahs to wake the body
4. Make du'a — this is the time Allah's response is most certain
5. Be consistent, even if it is only two rak'ahs

The Prophet said: 'Do not abandon night prayer — for it was the practice of the righteous before you, and it is a means of drawing near to your Lord.' (Jami' al-Tirmidhi 3549)
thursday.source: Sahih Muslim, Hadith 1163; Fiqh us-Sunnah by Sayyid Sabiq; Qiyam al-Layl by Muhammad Nasir al-Din al-Albani

thursday.title: Fiqh of Witr — The Seal of Night Prayers
thursday.arabic_text: اجْعَلُوا آخِرَ صَلَاتِكُمْ بِاللَّيْلِ وِتْرًا
thursday.english_text: Make Witr the last of your prayers at night.
thursday.lesson:
Witr is a minimum of one rak'ah prayed after Isha, before Fajr. It is wajib (obligatory) according to the Hanafi school and Sunnah Mu'akkadah according to the majority. The Prophet never abandoned Witr — whether at home or traveling. The preferred format: 11 rak'ahs total (8 + 3), or 5 together, or simply 1.

For corps members who cannot pray the full night prayer: at minimum, pray Witr before sleeping. It is the seal of the day's worship and takes less than two minutes.
thursday.extra_notes:
Du'a al-Qunut (in Witr):
Recited in the last rak'ah of Witr, after ruku' or before it depending on madhab:
'Allahummah-dini feeman hadayt...' (O Allah, guide me among those You have guided...)
This is the established Qunut of Witr from the teaching of the Prophet to al-Hasan ibn Ali.
thursday.source: Sahih al-Bukhari, Hadith 998; Fiqh us-Sunnah by Sayyid Sabiq; Sunan an-Nasa'i, Hadith 1745

friday.title: The Reward of Jumu'ah — What You Gain Each Week
friday.arabic_text: مَنِ اغْتَسَلَ يَوْمَ الْجُمُعَةِ وَلَبِسَ مِنْ أَحْسَنِ ثِيَابِهِ وَمَسَّ مِنْ طِيبٍ إِنْ كَانَ عِنْدَهُ ثُمَّ أَتَى الْجُمُعَةَ فَلَمْ يَتَخَطَّ أَعْنَاقَ النَّاسِ ثُمَّ صَلَّى مَا كُتِبَ لَهُ ثُمَّ أَنْصَتَ إِذَا خَرَجَ إِمَامُهُ حَتَّى يَفْرُغَ مِنْ صَلَاتِهِ كَانَتْ كَفَّارَةً لِمَا بَيْنَهَا وَبَيْنَ الْجُمُعَةِ الَّتِي قَبْلَهَا
friday.english_text: Whoever bathes on Friday, wears his best clothes, applies perfume if he has it, goes to Jumu'ah, does not step over people's necks, prays what is written for him, and is silent when the imam comes out — all of this is expiation for his sins between that Friday and the previous Friday.
friday.lesson: This hadith is an extraordinary gift: every Friday, all minor sins of the previous week are wiped clean — simply through proper Jumu'ah attendance. The conditions: ghusl, best clothes, optional perfume, early arrival, not disrupting others, praying nafl, listening to the khutbah. For a corps member making mistakes and struggling with consistency — this weekly reset is one of the greatest mercies of Islam.
friday.extra_notes: Note: Scholars clarify that this expiation covers minor sins, not major sins (kaba'ir). Major sins require specific tawbah. But for the everyday accumulation of small errors in speech, thought, and action — Jumu'ah wipes the slate clean every week. This is why the Sahaba were so eager to attend.
friday.source: Musnad Ahmad, Hadith 7815; Sunan Abi Dawud, Hadith 343; Classified as Hasan by al-Albani

friday.title: Friday Azkar — Du'a for the Muslim Ummah
friday.arabic_text: اللَّهُمَّ أَصْلِحْ أُمَّةَ مُحَمَّدٍ، اللَّهُمَّ فَرِّجْ عَنْ أُمَّةِ مُحَمَّدٍ، اللَّهُمَّ ارْحَمْ أُمَّةَ مُحَمَّدٍ
friday.english_text: O Allah, reform the Ummah of Muhammad. O Allah, relieve the distress of the Ummah of Muhammad. O Allah, have mercy on the Ummah of Muhammad.
friday.transliteration: Allahumma aslih ummata Muhammad, Allahumma farrij 'an ummati Muhammad, Allahumma-rham ummata Muhammad.
friday.benefits: Making du'a for the entire Muslim Ummah on Friday — while Muslims across the world are gathering for Jumu'ah — is a form of spiritual solidarity that transcends borders, languages, and ethnicities. This du'a is rooted in prophetic practice and is especially powerful when the Ummah faces hardship. A corps member who makes this du'a every Friday is connected to 1.8 billion Muslims in a single supplication.
friday.source: Jami' al-Tirmidhi, Hadith 3940; al-Adhkar by Imam an-Nawawi; Authenticated in Silsilah as-Sahihah by al-Albani (2265)

saturday.title: Abu Dharr al-Ghifari (RA) — The Courageous Truth-Speaker
saturday.arabic_text: مَا أَظَلَّتِ الْخَضْرَاءُ وَلَا أَقَلَّتِ الْغَبْرَاءُ أَصْدَقَ لَهْجَةً مِنْ أَبِي ذَرٍّ
saturday.english_text: The green canopy (sky) has not shaded, nor the brown earth borne, a man more truthful in speech than Abu Dharr.
saturday.lesson:
Abu Dharr al-Ghifari (RA) was a man from the Ghifar tribe — known as a tribe of highway robbers — who heard of the Prophet, traveled to Makkah alone, and immediately accepted Islam when he met him. He was so bold in his faith that he publicly declared his Islam in the Haram, the Prophet's compound, knowing he would be beaten.

Later, Abu Dharr's opposition to the accumulation of wealth without distribution to the poor brought him into conflict with some Umayyad rulers, and he died in exile at ar-Rabadha — alone, except for his wife and son. The Prophet's testimony about his absolute truthfulness stands as his eternal epitaph.

Lesson: Speaking truth to power comes at a cost. But the Muslim who does so sincerely, consistently, and with knowledge — like Abu Dharr — earns a testimony from the Prophet himself.
saturday.source: Jami' al-Tirmidhi, Hadith 3801; Al-Isabah fi Tamyiz as-Sahabah by Ibn Hajar; Siyar A'lam an-Nubala by Imam adh-Dhahabi

saturday.title: Safiyyah bint Huyayy (RA) — Nobility Through Islam
saturday.arabic_text: أَنَا بِنْتُ سَيِّدَيْنِ وَزَوْجَةُ نَبِيٍّ
saturday.english_text: I am the daughter of two masters and the wife of a prophet.
saturday.lesson:
Safiyyah bint Huyayy (RA) was the daughter of Huyayy ibn Akhtab, the chief of the Banu Nadir, and a descendant of the Prophet Harun (Aaron, AS). After her father and first husband were killed in the aftermath of the Battle of Khaybar, she was taken as a prisoner of war and the Prophet chose to free her and marry her.

Once, when a woman taunted her about her Jewish origins, Safiyyah came to the Prophet in tears. He told her to say: 'My father is Harun, my uncle is Musa, and my husband is Muhammad — so how are you better than me?' Her identity in Islam was defined not by ethnicity but by her noble lineage of prophets and her connection to the Messenger of Allah.

Lesson: Tribal, ethnic, and racial pride are explicitly rejected in Islam. 'The most noble of you before Allah is the most righteous of you.' (Quran 49:13). Your posting state, your tribe, your language — none of these define your Islamic worth.
saturday.source: Al-Isabah fi Tamyiz as-Sahabah by Ibn Hajar; Siyar A'lam an-Nubala by Imam adh-Dhahabi; As-Seerah an-Nabawiyyah by Ibn Hisham

sunday.title: The Battle of Badr — When the Outnumbered Won
sunday.arabic_text: كَمْ مِنْ فِئَةٍ قَلِيلَةٍ غَلَبَتْ فِئَةً كَثِيرَةً بِإِذْنِ اللَّهِ
sunday.english_text: How many a small company has overcome a large company by permission of Allah. (Quran 2:249)
sunday.lesson:
The Battle of Badr (2 AH) was the first major military confrontation between the Muslims and the Quraysh. The Muslims numbered 313 fighters against an army of 1,000 well-equipped Quraysh warriors. Allah sent 3,000 angels to assist the believers, and the Muslims won a decisive victory.

The Quran references Badr repeatedly as the proof that numbers do not determine victory — sincerity, taqwa, and reliance on Allah do. For the Muslim corps member who feels outnumbered, under-resourced, or overwhelmed by circumstances: Badr is the reminder that the mathematics of this world are not the mathematics of Allah.
sunday.source: Quran 3:123-125; Quran 8:5-19; Tafsir Ibn Kathir, Surah al-Anfal; As-Seerah an-Nabawiyyah by Ibn Hisham

sunday.title: The Battle of Uhud — Lessons in Obedience and Recovery
sunday.arabic_text: وَلَقَدْ صَدَقَكُمُ اللَّهُ وَعْدَهُ إِذْ تَحُسُّونَهُم بِإِذْنِهِ حَتَّىٰ إِذَا فَشِلْتُمْ وَتَنَازَعْتُمْ فِي الْأَمْرِ
sunday.english_text: And Allah had certainly fulfilled His promise to you when you were cutting them down by His permission — until you lost heart and disputed about the matter. (Quran 3:152)
sunday.lesson:
The Battle of Uhud began as a Muslim victory — until a group of archers abandoned their assigned position to collect booty, directly against the Prophet's command. The Quraysh cavalry turned around, attacked from behind, and the Muslims suffered a serious defeat with 70 companions martyred, including Hamzah.

The Quran uses Uhud not as a story of failure but as a lesson in discipline, obedience, and resilience. The Muslims recovered, maintained formation, and ultimately the Quraysh retreated without achieving their objective.

Lesson for corps members: Disobeying clear guidance — of Allah, of the Prophet, of legitimate authority — in pursuit of short-term gain leads to long-term loss. The archers of Uhud had victory in their hands and lost it to impatience.
sunday.source: Quran 3:121-179; As-Seerah an-Nabawiyyah by Ibn Hisham; Tafsir Ibn Kathir, Surah Al Imran

monday.title: Hadith on Gratitude to People
monday.arabic_text: لَا يَشْكُرُ اللَّهَ مَنْ لَا يَشْكُرُ النَّاسَ
monday.english_text: Whoever does not thank people has not thanked Allah.
monday.reported_by: Narrated by Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him). Recorded in Sunan Abi Dawud (4811) and Jami' al-Tirmidhi (1954), classified as Sahih.
monday.lesson: Gratitude to Allah is incomplete without gratitude to the people through whom Allah delivers His blessings. Your parents, teachers, supervisors, community elders, and even the colleague who helped you — thanking them is part of your worship. A corps member who expresses sincere thanks to their supervisor, their host family, or the local community they serve is practicing a dimension of shukr (gratitude) directly taught by the Prophet.
monday.source: Sunan Abi Dawud, Hadith 4811; Jami' al-Tirmidhi, Hadith 1954; Riyad as-Salihin, Chapter on Gratitude

monday.title: Hadith on the Blessed Hand
monday.arabic_text: الْيَدُ الْعُلْيَا خَيْرٌ مِنَ الْيَدِ السُّفْلَى، وَالْيَدُ الْعُلْيَا هِيَ الْمُنْفِقَةُ
monday.english_text: The upper hand is better than the lower hand. The upper hand is the one that gives.
monday.chain_of_narration: Ibn Umar (RA) → Nafi' → Malik ibn Anas
monday.reported_by: Narrated by Ibn Umar (may Allah be pleased with him). Recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari (1429) and Sahih Muslim (1033).
monday.lesson: Being a giver is better than being a receiver. This does not only mean money — it means giving time, knowledge, effort, emotional support, and service. Every corps member is in a position to give: give your skills to your community, give your time to those in need, give your knowledge to those who lack it. The giver's hand is the elevated hand.
monday.source: Sahih al-Bukhari, Hadith 1429; Sahih Muslim, Hadith 1033; Riyad as-Salihin, Chapter on Spending

tuesday.title: Morning Dhikr — A'udhu billahi minas-shaytanir-rajim
tuesday.arabic_text: أَعُوذُ بِاللَّهِ مِنَ الشَّيْطَانِ الرَّجِيمِ
tuesday.english_text: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shaytan.
tuesday.transliteration: A'udhu billahi minas-shaytanir-rajim.
tuesday.benefits: This ta'awwudh (seeking refuge) is prescribed before Quran recitation, before entering the toilet, when angry, when experiencing whispers of doubt, and at other key moments. The Prophet said: 'If a person says this when angry, his anger will leave him.' (Sahih al-Bukhari 3282). Shaytan is the declared enemy of every human — seeking refuge in Allah from him is not optional but a constant spiritual defense.
tuesday.source: Quran 16:98; Sahih al-Bukhari, Hadith 3282; al-Adhkar by Imam an-Nawawi

tuesday.title: Du'a for Travelling
tuesday.arabic_text: اللَّهُ أَكْبَرُ اللَّهُ أَكْبَرُ اللَّهُ أَكْبَرُ، سُبْحَانَ الَّذِي سَخَّرَ لَنَا هَٰذَا وَمَا كُنَّا لَهُ مُقْرِنِينَ، وَإِنَّا إِلَىٰ رَبِّنَا لَمُنقَلِبُونَ
tuesday.english_text: Allah is the Greatest (3x). Glory be to the One who has placed this at our service, for we could not have done so ourselves, and indeed to our Lord we shall return.
tuesday.transliteration: Allahu Akbar (3x). Subhanal-ladhi sakhkhara lana hadha wa ma kunna lahu muqrinin, wa inna ila Rabbina lamunqalibun.
tuesday.benefits: This is the Sunnah du'a when mounting any vehicle or beginning a journey — taken from Quran 43:13-14 and authenticated in Sahih Muslim. A corps member traveling between states, to their posting, or on CDS assignments should recite this upon boarding any vehicle. It acknowledges Allah's gift of transportation and reminds us that every journey may be our last.
tuesday.source: Sahih Muslim, Hadith 1342; Quran 43:13-14; Hisn al-Muslim by Sa'id al-Qahtani

wednesday.title: The Prophet's Description of Allah — The Hadith of Jibril
wednesday.arabic_text: الإِيمَانُ أَنْ تُؤْمِنَ بِاللَّهِ وَمَلَائِكَتِهِ وَكُتُبِهِ وَرُسُلِهِ وَالْيَوْمِ الآخِرِ وَتُؤْمِنَ بِالْقَدَرِ خَيْرِهِ وَشَرِّهِ
wednesday.english_text: Iman is to believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and to believe in divine decree — both its good and its evil.
wednesday.lesson:
The Hadith of Jibril (Sahih Muslim 8) is considered the most comprehensive summary of Islamic theology. In a single conversation, the angel Jibril in human form asked the Prophet about Islam, Iman, and Ihsan — and the Prophet answered. This hadith serves as the foundation of Islamic theology and is studied by scholars across all four madhabs as the basis of 'aqeedah (creed).

The six pillars of Iman summarized: (1) Allah, (2) Angels, (3) Books, (4) Messengers, (5) Last Day, (6) Divine Decree. Every Muslim must know and believe in all six with certainty.
wednesday.extra_notes:
Q: Why is this called the Hadith of Jibril?
A: Because the questioner was revealed to be the angel Jibril (AS) himself, who came in human form to teach the companions. The Prophet said after he left: 'That was Jibril, who came to teach you your religion.' This hadith therefore represents divine instruction on the essentials of faith.
wednesday.source: Sahih Muslim, Hadith 8; Sahih al-Bukhari, Hadith 50; Jami' al-Ulum wal-Hikam by Ibn Rajab, Hadith 2

wednesday.title: The Five Pillars of Islam — Al-Arkan al-Khamsah
wednesday.arabic_text: بُنِيَ الإِسْلامُ عَلَى خَمْسٍ: شَهَادَةِ أَنْ لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ وَأَنَّ مُحَمَّدًا رَسُولُ اللَّهِ، وَإِقَامِ الصَّلاةِ، وَإِيتَاءِ الزَّكَاةِ، وَحَجِّ الْبَيْتِ، وَصَوْمِ رَمَضَانَ
wednesday.english_text: Islam is built on five: testifying that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, establishing prayer, giving Zakah, Hajj to the House, and fasting Ramadan.
wednesday.lesson: The Five Pillars are the structural frame of the Muslim's practical religious life. Each pillar has a unique function: Shahada (declaration of faith and identity), Salah (direct connection with Allah five times daily), Zakah (financial purification and social solidarity), Sawm (annual discipline, gratitude, and empathy with the poor), and Hajj (universal gathering and submission to Allah). A Muslim who fulfills all five has built a complete structure of worship.
wednesday.extra_notes:
Practical state for corps members:
- Shahada: Renewed daily in every prayer
- Salah: Five times daily — the non-negotiable minimum
- Zakah: Calculated annually on qualifying savings
- Sawm: Ramadan every year — prepare well in advance
- Hajj: A lifetime goal — begin saving and planning
wednesday.source: Sahih al-Bukhari, Hadith 8; Sahih Muslim, Hadith 16; Jami' al-Ulum wal-Hikam by Ibn Rajab, Hadith 3

thursday.title: Fiqh of Ramadan — Preparation and Key Rulings
thursday.arabic_text: شَهْرُ رَمَضَانَ الَّذِي أُنزِلَ فِيهِ الْقُرْآنُ هُدًى لِّلنَّاسِ
thursday.english_text: The month of Ramadan in which was revealed the Quran — guidance for the people. (Quran 2:185)
thursday.lesson:
Ramadan is the ninth month of the Islamic lunar calendar — the month of fasting from Fajr to Maghrib, intensified worship, Tarawih prayers, increased Quran recitation, and seeking Laylat al-Qadr. For the corps member: Ramadan may fall during your service year. Prepare well: inform your supervisor, arrange your work schedule, plan your Quran completion, identify a Tarawih location.

Key rulings: Suhoor (pre-dawn meal) is Sunnah. Iftar (breaking fast) should be immediate at Maghrib. Zakat al-Fitr is due at the end of Ramadan. Eid al-Fitr follows the completion of Ramadan.
thursday.extra_notes:
Things that invalidate the fast: eating, drinking, intentional vomiting, marital relations, and injection of nutritious substances (majority view). Things that do NOT invalidate the fast: brushing teeth (if no toothpaste is swallowed), using miswak, eye drops, ear drops, injections that are not nutritious (insulin, etc. per contemporary scholars), unintentional swallowing of water during ghusl.

Q: Can I fast Ramadan while sick?
A: If fasting causes significant harm, it is permissible (and may be obligatory) to break your fast and make up the days later. Allah says: 'Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship.' (Quran 2:185)
thursday.source: Fiqh us-Sunnah by Sayyid Sabiq, Vol. 3; Al-Fiqh al-Islami wa Adillatuh by Wahbah az-Zuhayli; Sharh al-Mumti' by Shaykh Ibn al-'Uthaymeen

thursday.title: Fiqh of I'tikaf — Seclusion in the Masjid
thursday.arabic_text: وَلَا تُبَاشِرُوهُنَّ وَأَنتُمْ عَاكِفُونَ فِي الْمَسَاجِدِ
thursday.english_text: And do not have relations with them while you are in retreat in the mosques. (Quran 2:187)
thursday.lesson:
I'tikaf is the Sunnah of spending the last ten nights of Ramadan in the masjid, devoted entirely to worship, du'a, and seeking Laylat al-Qadr. The Prophet never abandoned this Sunnah, and when he missed it one Ramadan, he made it up in Shawwal. The person in i'tikaf does not leave the masjid except for necessity, does not engage in trade or business, and dedicates those ten nights entirely to Allah.

For corps members: Even if a full ten-day i'tikaf is not possible due to work obligations, spending the odd nights of the last ten in extra worship and seeking Laylat al-Qadr is achievable and profoundly rewarding.
thursday.extra_notes:
Laylat al-Qadr: 'The Night of Power is better than a thousand months' (Quran 97:3) — worship on this night equals more than 83 years of worship. The Prophet directed: seek it in the odd nights of the last ten of Ramadan (21st, 23rd, 25th, 27th, 29th). The 27th night is most commonly believed to be Laylat al-Qadr in many traditions.

Du'a for Laylat al-Qadr: 'Allahumma innaka 'afuwwun tuhibbul-'afwa fa'fu 'anni' — O Allah, You are Pardoning and love to pardon, so pardon me. (Jami' al-Tirmidhi 3513)
thursday.source: Sahih al-Bukhari, Hadith 2026; Sahih Muslim, Hadith 1167; Al-Fiqh al-Islami wa Adillatuh by Wahbah az-Zuhayli

friday.title: What to Do Between Jumu'ah and Asr
friday.arabic_text: فَإِذَا قُضِيَتِ الصَّلَاةُ فَانتَشِرُوا فِي الْأَرْضِ وَابْتَغُوا مِن فَضْلِ اللَّهِ
friday.english_text: And when the prayer is concluded, disperse throughout the land and seek from the bounty of Allah. (Quran 62:10)
friday.lesson: The Quran explicitly transitions from Jumu'ah to worldly activity — seek rizq after prayer. But the hours between Jumu'ah and Asr on Friday are among the most blessed of the week for ibadah. The recommended acts: pray four rak'ahs of nafl after Jumu'ah (or two at home), make du'a in the final hour before Maghrib, visit a Muslim brother or sister, review your Quran, and make the most of the remaining blessed time before the day ends.
friday.extra_notes:
A recommended Friday schedule:
- Pre-Fajr: Tahajjud, recite end of Surah al-Kahf
- After Fajr: Morning adhkar
- Morning: Begin or continue Surah al-Kahf reading
- Before Jumu'ah: Ghusl, best clothes, go early
- Jumu'ah: Arrive early, nafl, listen to khutbah, two rak'ahs of Jumu'ah
- After Jumu'ah: Four rak'ahs nafl, lunch
- Afternoon: Last hour before Maghrib — intensive du'a
- Evening: Evening adhkar, extra dhikr and salawat
friday.source: Quran 62:10; Sahih Muslim, Hadith 882 (nafl after Jumu'ah); Riyad as-Salihin, Chapter on Friday

friday.title: Friday Azkar — Abundant Salawat on the Prophet
friday.arabic_text: إِنَّ مِنْ أَفْضَلِ أَيَّامِكُمْ يَوْمَ الْجُمُعَةِ، فَأَكْثِرُوا عَلَيَّ مِنَ الصَّلَاةِ فِيهِ
friday.english_text: Indeed among the best of your days is Friday, so send abundant salawat upon me on it.
friday.transliteration: Allahumma salli 'ala Muhammadin wa 'ala ali Muhammad... (abundantly throughout Friday)
friday.benefits: The Prophet specifically commanded abundant salawat on Fridays. Every salawat upon the Prophet returns to him and Allah sends ten blessings on the one who sent it. Making salawat 100 times on Friday is a well-known practice of the pious predecessors, recommended by scholars including Imam al-Shafi'i and Ibn al-Qayyim. Set a target for Friday — 100 or more — and keep count.
friday.source: Sunan Abi Dawud, Hadith 1047; Sunan an-Nasa'i; Jala' al-Afham by Ibn al-Qayyim (comprehensive book on salawat)

saturday.title: Abdullah ibn Abbas (RA) — The Scholar of the Ummah
saturday.arabic_text: اللَّهُمَّ عَلِّمْهُ الْكِتَابَ
saturday.english_text: O Allah, teach him the Book.
saturday.lesson:
Abdullah ibn Abbas (RA) was the Prophet's cousin and was just ten years old when the Prophet passed away — yet he became the greatest exegete (mufassir) of the Quran in Islamic history. The Prophet prayed for him: 'O Allah, teach him the Book and give him understanding of the religion.' Allah answered this du'a.

Ibn Abbas would sit at the door of a companion's house all night, wrapped in his cloak, waiting for him to wake up so he could ask a single question of knowledge. His dedication to learning is legendary among scholars.

Lesson: Age is not a barrier to scholarship. Dedication, patience in seeking knowledge, and reliance on Allah's guidance — these are the tools. Every Muslim corps member should be a student of Islamic knowledge throughout their service year, even informally.
saturday.source: Sahih al-Bukhari, Hadith 75; Jami' al-Tirmidhi, Hadith 3824; Siyar A'lam an-Nubala by Imam adh-Dhahabi

saturday.title: Umm Habibah Ramlah bint Abi Sufyan (RA) — Faith Against All Odds
saturday.arabic_text: اللَّهُمَّ أَمْتِعْنِي بِزَوْجِي رَسُولِ اللَّهِ
saturday.english_text: O Allah, let me enjoy my husband, the Messenger of Allah.
saturday.lesson:
Umm Habibah (RA) emigrated to Abyssinia with her husband Ubaydullah ibn Jahsh, fleeing Quraysh persecution. In Abyssinia, her husband apostatized and became a Christian, dying as one. She was left alone in a foreign land — a widow, far from family, unable to return to Makkah without risking her life. Yet she maintained her faith with extraordinary steadiness.

The Prophet proposed to her through the Negus (King of Abyssinia) by letter, and she married the Prophet without her father's presence — the Negus himself served as wali. She eventually returned to Madinah with honor.

Lesson: The Muslim woman alone in a foreign land, facing abandonment or social pressure, finds her model in Umm Habibah. Faith held firm in isolation is rewarded by Allah in ways that no human connection could provide.
saturday.source: Sahih Muslim, Hadith 1475; Al-Isabah fi Tamyiz as-Sahabah by Ibn Hajar; Siyar A'lam an-Nubala by Imam adh-Dhahabi

sunday.title: The Hijrah — Migration for Allah's Sake
sunday.arabic_text: وَمَن يُهَاجِرْ فِي سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ يَجِدْ فِي الْأَرْضِ مُرَاغَمًا كَثِيرًا وَسَعَةً
sunday.english_text: And whoever emigrates for the cause of Allah will find on earth many locations and abundance. (Quran 4:100)
sunday.lesson:
The Hijrah from Makkah to Madinah in 622 CE was the pivotal moment in Islamic history — so significant that the Islamic calendar begins from it. The Prophet and Abu Bakr left everything they owned, traveled through dangerous terrain, hid in a cave (Thawr), and arrived in Madinah to build the first true Islamic community.

Every Ansari (Madinah host) shared their home and wealth with the Muhajirin (Makkah emigrants) without resentment. The bond of brotherhood established between them — al-mu'akhat (fraternal pairing) — is described in the Quran as a sign of true faith (Quran 59:9).

For corps members: Your posting to another state is a small hijrah. Use it to grow, to build bonds, and to serve — just as the Muhajirin used their displacement to build the greatest community in human history.
sunday.source: Quran 4:100; Quran 59:9; As-Seerah an-Nabawiyyah by Ibn Hisham; Al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah by Ibn Kathir

sunday.title: The Treaty of Hudaybiyyah — When Victory Looks Like Defeat
sunday.arabic_text: إِنَّا فَتَحْنَا لَكَ فَتْحًا مُّبِينًا
sunday.english_text: Indeed, We have given you a clear conquest. (Quran 48:1)
sunday.lesson:
In 6 AH, the Prophet and 1,400 companions traveled to Makkah for Umrah but were stopped at Hudaybiyyah. The treaty that followed appeared deeply unfavorable to the Muslims: they had to return without performing Umrah, return any Muslim who came from Makkah, and agree to a ten-year truce on Quraysh's terms. Umar ibn al-Khattab was furious.

Yet Allah revealed: 'We have given you a clear conquest.' Within two years, the treaty had opened the door to mass conversions, strategic alliances, and ultimately the Conquest of Makkah in 8 AH — the greatest expansion of Islam in its early period.

Lesson: What appears as loss or unfairness from your perspective may be the beginning of Allah's greatest plan for you. The corps member who receives a 'bad' posting, a difficult supervisor, or an undesirable assignment may be standing at their personal Hudaybiyyah — the gateway to something greater.
sunday.source: Quran 48:1-29; As-Seerah an-Nabawiyyah by Ibn Hisham; Tafsir Ibn Kathir, Surah al-Fath

monday.title: Hadith on Time and Its Value
monday.arabic_text: نِعْمَتَانِ مَغْبُونٌ فِيهِمَا كَثِيرٌ مِنَ النَّاسِ: الصِّحَّةُ وَالْفَرَاغُ
monday.english_text: Two blessings in which many people incur loss: health and free time.
monday.transliteration: Ni'matani maghbunun fihima kathirum minan-naas: as-sihhatu wal-faragh.
monday.reported_by: Narrated by Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him). Recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari (6412).
monday.lesson: Health and free time are the two most squandered blessings. The service year offers both — and both will not last. A corps member with energy, time, and an entire community to serve who wastes the year on entertainment and idleness is incurring a spiritual loss they may not fully feel until the Day of Reckoning. Time management is an Islamic obligation.
monday.source: Sahih al-Bukhari, Hadith 6412; Jami' al-Ulum wal-Hikam by Ibn Rajab; Riyad as-Salihin, Chapter on Time

monday.title: Hadith on Cleanliness
monday.english_text: Cleanliness is half of faith.
monday.reported_by: Narrated by Abu Malik al-Ash'ari (may Allah be pleased with him). Recorded in Sahih Muslim (223).
monday.lesson: Taharah (ritual and physical purity) is not merely hygienic practice — it is a pillar of Islamic worship. Wudu before prayer, ghusl when required, keeping the body, clothing, and living space clean — all are acts of worship. A corps member who maintains cleanliness in their accommodation, workspace, and personal appearance is fulfilling half of their faith in every moment of the day.
monday.source: Sahih Muslim, Hadith 223; Riyad as-Salihin, Chapter on Purity; Fiqh us-Sunnah by Sayyid Sabiq

tuesday.title: Du'a When Seeing Something Pleasing
tuesday.arabic_text: الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ الَّذِي بِنِعْمَتِهِ تَتِمُّ الصَّالِحَاتُ
tuesday.english_text: All praise is due to Allah by Whose blessing righteous deeds are completed.
tuesday.transliteration: Alhamdulillahil-ladhi bi-ni'matihi tatimmus-salihat.
tuesday.benefits: When something good happens, say this. When you receive good news, say this. When you complete a task successfully, say this. It attributes every good outcome to Allah's blessing rather than your own ability. Paired with 'Alhamdulillah' in difficulty ('Alhamdulillah 'ala kulli hal'), this pair of expressions of gratitude covers every state the believer passes through.
tuesday.source: Sunan Ibn Majah, Hadith 3803; al-Adhkar by Imam an-Nawawi; Hisn al-Muslim by Sa'id al-Qahtani

tuesday.title: Du'a When Seeing Something Displeasing
tuesday.arabic_text: الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ عَلَى كُلِّ حَالٍ
tuesday.english_text: All praise is due to Allah in every state.
tuesday.transliteration: Alhamdulillahi 'ala kulli hal.
tuesday.benefits: Praising Allah in difficulty is not denial of pain — it is the highest expression of trust in Allah's wisdom and plan. The Prophet praised Allah even at the death of his son Ibrahim. Saying 'Alhamdulillah' when things go wrong is one of the most powerful acts of worship because it costs the most — and earns the most. Corps members facing disappointments, delays, and hardships should attach this dhikr to every difficulty.
tuesday.source: Sunan Ibn Majah, Hadith 3803; Riyad as-Salihin, Chapter on Gratitude; al-Adhkar by Imam an-Nawawi

wednesday.title: Tazkiyat an-Nafs — Purification of the Soul
wednesday.arabic_text: قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَن زَكَّاهَا وَقَدْ خَابَ مَن دَسَّاهَا
wednesday.english_text: He has succeeded who purifies it (the soul). And he has failed who corrupts it. (Quran 91:9-10)
wednesday.lesson:
Tazkiyat an-Nafs (purification of the soul) is one of the primary objectives of the Prophet's mission (Quran 62:2). The soul has states: the al-nafs al-ammara bis-su' (the soul that commands evil), al-nafs al-lawwama (the self-reproaching soul that recognizes its faults), and al-nafs al-mutma'innah (the soul at peace). The goal of every Muslim is to move from the first through the second to the third.

For corps members: The service year is a spiritual crucible. Away from your normal environment and supports, your true character is revealed and tested. Use this year to identify your spiritual weaknesses and work on them — this is the work of tazkiyah.
wednesday.extra_notes:
Tools of tazkiyah:
1. Regular tawbah and istighfar
2. Fasting voluntary fasts beyond Ramadan
3. Night prayer (qiyam al-layl)
4. Keeping righteous company
5. Reading Quran with reflection (tadabbur)
6. Dhikr throughout the day
7. Giving sadaqah generously
8. Studying the seerah (Prophet's biography)
wednesday.source: Tafsir Ibn Kathir, Quran 91:9-10; Madarij as-Salikin by Ibn al-Qayyim; Minhaj al-Qasidin by Ibn Qudamah

wednesday.title: Al-Mahabbah — Love of Allah as the Foundation of Worship
wednesday.english_text: Those who believe are stronger in love for Allah. (Quran 2:165)
wednesday.lesson:
Love of Allah (mahabbah) is the engine of worship. When a person truly loves Allah, obedience is not a burden but a pleasure, and sin is not an attraction but an offense to the beloved. Ibn al-Qayyim describes love of Allah as the foundation of the entire spiritual journey. Signs of true love of Allah: following the Prophet's Sunnah, preferring Allah's pleasure over people's pleasure, yearning for the meeting with Allah, and feeling pain when one falls short in worship.

The test of love: 'Say, if you love Allah, follow me — and Allah will love you.' (Quran 3:31). Love of Allah and love of the Prophet are inseparable in Islam.
wednesday.extra_notes:
Q: How do I increase my love for Allah?
A: Ibn al-Qayyim lists ten causes: reciting the Quran with tadabbur, drawing near to Allah through nafl after fulfilling obligatory worship, continual dhikr, preferring what Allah loves in every situation, contemplating Allah's names and attributes, witnessing Allah's blessings, breaking the heart of pride, and spending time in solitary worship.
wednesday.source: Tafsir Ibn Kathir, Quran 2:165; Madarij as-Salikin by Ibn al-Qayyim; Al-Fawa'id by Ibn al-Qayyim

thursday.title: Fiqh of Da'wah — Calling Others to Islam
thursday.arabic_text: ادْعُ إِلَىٰ سَبِيلِ رَبِّكَ بِالْحِكْمَةِ وَالْمَوْعِظَةِ الْحَسَنَةِ
thursday.english_text: Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good instruction. (Quran 16:125)
thursday.lesson:
Da'wah (calling to Islam and to goodness) is a collective obligation upon Muslims. The Quran outlines its methodology: hikma (wisdom — saying the right thing at the right time to the right person), maw'izah hasanah (good instruction — using beautiful, compassionate language), and mujadalah billatee hiya ahsan (arguing in the best way — using logic and evidence without personal attacks).

For corps members: You are ambassadors of Islam in your posting communities. Your character, your work ethic, your honesty — these are da'wah before a single word is spoken. The Prophet said: 'Convey from me even if it is one verse.' (Sahih al-Bukhari 3461)
thursday.extra_notes:
Da'wah through character (da'wah bil-hal):
The most powerful da'wah is lived example. Being the most honest person at work, the most kind neighbor, the most reliable colleague — these speak louder than any lecture. Many of the earliest converts to Islam in Makkah were moved by the Prophet's character before they even heard his message.

Practical da'wah for corps members: sharing Islamic knowledge in CDS meetings, organizing educational events through MCAN, being available to answer questions about Islam from non-Muslim colleagues.
thursday.source: Tafsir Ibn Kathir, Quran 16:125; Fiqh ad-Da'wah by Yusuf al-Qaradawi; Sahih al-Bukhari, Hadith 3461

thursday.title: Fiqh of Interfaith Relations — Justice and Kindness to Non-Muslims
thursday.arabic_text: لَّا يَنْهَاكُمُ اللَّهُ عَنِ الَّذِينَ لَمْ يُقَاتِلُوكُمْ فِي الدِّينِ وَلَمْ يُخْرِجُوكُم مِّن دِيَارِكُمْ أَن تَبَرُّوهُمْ وَتُقْسِطُوا إِلَيْهِمْ
thursday.english_text: Allah does not forbid you from those who do not fight you for religion and do not expel you from your homes — from being righteous toward them and acting justly toward them. (Quran 60:8)
thursday.lesson:
The Quran explicitly permits and encourages justice and kindness toward non-Muslims who are not hostile to Muslims. This includes: sharing food with non-Muslim neighbors, visiting their sick, accepting their gifts, working with them professionally, and treating them with full human dignity.

For corps members in multi-religious settings: the Islamic standard for dealing with non-Muslim colleagues and community members is birr (righteousness) and qist (justice) — not hostility, suspicion, or social avoidance.
thursday.extra_notes:
Common questions:
Q: Can I eat food prepared by non-Muslims?
A: Food prepared by non-Muslims is generally permissible unless it contains pork, carrion, or alcohol. Meat specifically must be halal-slaughtered. Vegetarian and seafood dishes from non-Muslim kitchens are generally permissible.

Q: Can I attend a non-Muslim colleague's celebration?
A: You may attend to maintain social bonds and show respect, as long as you do not participate in any religiously prohibited element (drinking alcohol, participating in prayers to other deities, etc.).
thursday.source: Tafsir Ibn Kathir, Quran 60:8; Al-Fiqh al-Islami wa Adillatuh by Wahbah az-Zuhayli; Fiqh al-Aqalliyyat al-Muslimah by Yusuf al-Qaradawi

friday.title: The Virtues of the First Row in Prayer
friday.arabic_text: لَوْ يَعْلَمُ النَّاسُ مَا فِي النِّدَاءِ وَالصَّفِّ الْأَوَّلِ ثُمَّ لَمْ يَجِدُوا إِلَّا أَنْ يَسْتَهِمُوا عَلَيْهِ لَاسْتَهَمُوا
friday.english_text: If people knew what was in the call to prayer and the first row, and could find no other way to get it except by drawing lots, they would draw lots.
friday.lesson: The first row in congregational prayer carries such enormous reward that the Prophet said people would draw lots for it if they knew its true value. For Jumu'ah especially — arriving early enough to pray in the first row is one of the most rewarding acts of the week. Yet most people arrive late and settle for the back. The Muslim who consistently occupies the first row in their masjid is among those maximizing their Friday reward.
friday.extra_notes:
Guidelines on rows:
- Men fill the front rows first; women fill the back rows
- Do not leave gaps in a row — fill them
- Children should not be placed in the front rows if they disrupt the prayer
- It is Sunnah to straighten rows before prayer begins
- The best row for men: the first (front)
- The best row for women: the last (according to the Prophet's words in Sahih Muslim 440)
friday.source: Sahih al-Bukhari, Hadith 615; Sahih Muslim, Hadith 437; Al-Mughni by Ibn Qudamah

friday.title: Friday Azkar — Renewing the Covenant
friday.arabic_text: أَشْهَدُ أَنْ لَّا إِلَهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ وَحْدَهُ لَا شَرِيكَ لَهُ وَأَشْهَدُ أَنَّ مُحَمَّدًا عَبْدُهُ وَرَسُولُهُ
friday.english_text: I bear witness that there is no god but Allah alone, without partner, and I bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and messenger.
friday.transliteration: Ashhadu an la ilaha illallahu wahdahu la shareeka lah, wa ashhadu anna Muhammadan 'abduhu wa rasuluh.
friday.benefits: The Shahada is not a statement made once at conversion — it is a living covenant renewed in every prayer, every adhan, and ideally daily with consciousness. On Friday, renewing the Shahada with full awareness of what it means — that you belong entirely to Allah and follow the Prophet exclusively — sets the tone for the week ahead. Say it slowly, feel its weight, and recommit to living by it.
friday.source: Sahih Muslim, Hadith 234; al-Adhkar by Imam an-Nawawi; Kitab at-Tawheed by Shaykh Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab

saturday.title: Khalid ibn al-Walid (RA) — The Sword of Allah
saturday.arabic_text: سَيْفٌ مِنْ سُيُوفِ اللَّهِ سَلَّهُ اللَّهُ عَلَى الْكُفَّارِ
saturday.english_text: A sword from the swords of Allah, which Allah has drawn against the disbelievers.
saturday.lesson:
Khalid ibn al-Walid was one of the greatest military commanders in history — yet he embraced Islam only in 8 AH, just two years before the Prophet's death. Before his conversion, he was the man who turned the tide against the Muslims at Uhud. After his conversion, he never lost a single battle — not one in over 100 engagements.

At his deathbed, Khalid wept. When asked why, he said he had fought in every battle but was dying in his bed — not as a martyr. He died pointing to the wounds on his body as evidence of his lifetime of service.

Lesson: It is never too late to turn your skills toward Allah's service. The same qualities that made Khalid formidable as an opponent made him invincible as a believer. Your professional expertise, deployed in sincere service to Allah, is your sword.
saturday.source: Sahih al-Bukhari, Hadith 4265; Al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah by Ibn Kathir; Siyar A'lam an-Nubala by Imam adh-Dhahabi

saturday.title: Umm Atiyyah al-Ansariyyah (RA) — The Healer of the Battlefield
saturday.arabic_text: غَزَوْتُ مَعَ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ سَبْعَ غَزَوَاتٍ أَخْلُفُهُمْ فِي رِحَالِهِمْ
saturday.english_text: I participated in seven battles with the Messenger of Allah, staying behind to tend their camps.
saturday.lesson:
Umm Atiyyah al-Ansariyyah (RA) was among the women who participated in multiple military expeditions — not in combat, but in providing essential medical, logistical, and care services. She treated the wounded, cooked food for the fighters, and cared for the sick. The Prophet explicitly permitted and encouraged women's participation in this support role.

She was also a specialist in the ghusl (washing) of deceased Muslim women, and narrated important hadith about Islamic funeral rites.

Lesson: Service to the Muslim community takes many forms. Not everyone is on the front line — but those who provide essential support are equally honored in Islamic history. The corps member providing community health services, administrative support, or educational assistance is following the model of Umm Atiyyah.
saturday.source: Sahih al-Bukhari, Hadith 2882; Sahih Muslim, Hadith 938; Al-Isabah fi Tamyiz as-Sahabah by Ibn Hajar

sunday.title: The Conquest of Makkah — Mercy After Victory
sunday.arabic_text: اذْهَبُوا فَأَنتُمُ الطُّلَقَاءُ
sunday.english_text: Go — you are free.
sunday.lesson:
In 8 AH, the Prophet entered Makkah at the head of 10,000 companions — the city that had tortured, expelled, boycotted, and killed his followers for 21 years. The Quraysh expected retribution. Instead, the Prophet announced a general amnesty: 'Go — you are free.'

Among those pardoned: Abu Sufyan who had led armies against the Muslims, Hind bint Utbah who had mutilated Hamzah's body, Wahshi who had killed Hamzah, and Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl. Almost all of them embraced Islam.

Lesson: Mercy and forgiveness in the moment of power is the highest expression of Islamic character. The corps member who forgives a colleague who wronged them, a community that was unwelcoming, or a supervisor who was unjust — is following the most powerful Sunnah of the Conquest.
sunday.source: As-Seerah an-Nabawiyyah by Ibn Hisham; Sahih al-Bukhari, references to Fath Makkah; Al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah by Ibn Kathir

sunday.title: The Farewell Sermon — The Prophet's Final Address
sunday.arabic_text: أَيُّهَا النَّاسُ إِنَّ دِمَاءَكُمْ وَأَمْوَالَكُمْ وَأَعْرَاضَكُمْ عَلَيْكُمْ حَرَامٌ
sunday.english_text: O people, your blood, your wealth, and your honor are sacred to one another.
sunday.lesson:
The Farewell Sermon (Khutbat al-Wada') was delivered on Hajj in 10 AH — the Prophet's final and most comprehensive public address. Before 100,000+ companions at Mount Arafah, he summarized the essential principles of Islam: the inviolability of human life, blood, and honor; the abolition of riba (usury); women's rights and the obligation of husbands; the obligation to follow the Quran and Sunnah; the equality of all people; and the universality of the Islamic message.

He ended with: 'Have I conveyed the message? O Allah, bear witness.' The companions responded: 'Yes.' This is the permanent standard for Muslim civil society — a charter for justice, dignity, and equality that predates modern human rights declarations by 1,400 years.
sunday.source: Sahih al-Bukhari, Hadith 1741; Sahih Muslim, Hadith 1218; As-Seerah an-Nabawiyyah by Ibn Hisham

monday.title: Hadith on Justice
monday.english_text: The scales of justice are in the right hand of the Most Merciful.
monday.chain_of_narration: Abdullah ibn Umar (RA) → Nafi' → multiple chains
monday.reported_by: Narrated by Abdullah ibn Umar (may Allah be pleased with him). Recorded in Sahih Muslim (1827).
monday.lesson: Justice (adl) is among the most fundamental principles of Islam, described as being in the hands of ar-Rahman Himself. The Prophet said the most beloved people to Allah on the Day of Judgment are the just leaders. For a Muslim corps member in any position of responsibility — team leader, project coordinator, classroom teacher — exercising justice is not merely professional best practice; it is a divine mandate.
monday.source: Sahih Muslim, Hadith 1827; Riyad as-Salihin, Chapter on Justice; Tafsir Ibn Kathir, Quran 4:135

monday.title: Hadith on Contentment (Qana'ah)
monday.arabic_text: قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَنْ أَسْلَمَ وَرُزِقَ كَفَافًا وَقَنَّعَهُ اللَّهُ بِمَا آتَاهُ
monday.english_text: Successful is the one who submits, is given sufficient provision, and Allah makes him content with what He has given him.
monday.transliteration: Qad aflaha man aslama wa ruzuqa kafaafan wa qanna'ahullahu bima atah.
monday.chain_of_narration: Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As (RA) → multiple chains
monday.reported_by: Narrated by Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As (may Allah be pleased with him). Recorded in Sahih Muslim (1054).
monday.lesson: Qana'ah (contentment) with what Allah has provided is a treasure greater than any worldly wealth. The Prophet said: 'Contentment is a never-failing treasure.' (al-Bayhaqi). For a corps member earning a modest allowance and surrounded by peers with more visible resources: contentment with halal provision is freedom. Discontentment poisons gratitude and opens the door to compromise.
monday.source: Sahih Muslim, Hadith 1054; Al-Bayhaqi, Shu'ab al-Iman; Riyad as-Salihin, Chapter on Contentment

tuesday.title: Dhikr of Tahleel — La ilaha illallah
tuesday.arabic_text: لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ
tuesday.english_text: There is no god but Allah.
tuesday.transliteration: La ilaha illallah.
tuesday.benefits: The Prophet said: 'The best dhikr is La ilaha illallah.' (Jami' al-Tirmidhi 3383). He also said: 'Whoever's last words are La ilaha illallah enters Paradise.' (Sunan Abi Dawud 3116). This phrase is the foundation of the entire deen — the first pillar, the entry point to Islam, and the last statement of the believer. Say it with full consciousness of its meaning: you are declaring that nothing and no one has the right to your worship, your deepest loyalty, or your ultimate surrender except Allah alone.
tuesday.source: Jami' al-Tirmidhi, Hadith 3383; Sunan Abi Dawud, Hadith 3116; al-Adhkar by Imam an-Nawawi

tuesday.title: Dhikr for the Last Ten Days of Ramadan
tuesday.arabic_text: اللَّهُمَّ إِنَّكَ عَفُوٌّ تُحِبُّ الْعَفْوَ فَاعْفُ عَنِّي
tuesday.english_text: O Allah, You are Pardoning and love to pardon, so pardon me.
tuesday.transliteration: Allahumma innaka 'afuwwun tuhibbul-'afwa fa'fu 'anni.
tuesday.benefits: Aisha (RA) asked the Prophet: if I know which night is Laylat al-Qadr, what should I say? He taught her this du'a. It focuses entirely on Allah's quality of 'afuw (pardoning) — which is even greater than maghfirah (forgiveness). Maghfirah forgives the sin and covers it; 'afuw erases it as though it never occurred. On the odd nights of the last ten of Ramadan and on Laylat al-Qadr itself, repeat this du'a abundantly.
tuesday.source: Jami' al-Tirmidhi, Hadith 3513 (Sahih); Musnad Ahmad; Hisn al-Muslim by Sa'id al-Qahtani

wednesday.title: Sabr — Patience as an Act of Tawheed
wednesday.english_text: And be patient — and your patience is only through Allah. (Quran 16:127)
wednesday.lesson:
Sabr (patience) in Islamic theology is not mere human endurance — it is a divine gift. The Quran says your patience itself comes from Allah. Ibn al-Qayyim describes three types of sabr: patience in obeying Allah, patience in refraining from what He has forbidden, and patience in accepting His divine decrees. The third type — patience in hardship — is the most difficult and has the greatest reward.

For corps members: patience in a difficult posting, with an unfair supervisor, in a community that doesn't respond to your efforts, or with health challenges — all of these are opportunities for sabr that earns the companionship of Allah (Quran 2:153: 'Allah is with the patient').
wednesday.extra_notes:
The reward of sabr:
'Those who are patient will be given their reward without account.' (Quran 39:10) — meaning immeasurable reward without a counting process. The scholars say this is the highest possible statement of reward in the Quran. Sabr is the one deed whose reward is limitless.
wednesday.source: Tafsir Ibn Kathir, Quran 16:127; Uddat as-Sabirin wa Dhakhirat ash-Shakirin by Ibn al-Qayyim; Madarij as-Salikin by Ibn al-Qayyim

wednesday.title: Shukr — Gratitude as Worship
wednesday.english_text: If you are grateful, I will surely increase you in favor. (Quran 14:7)
wednesday.lesson:
Shukr (gratitude) is among the highest stations of worship. Ibn al-Qayyim says the Islamic journey is summarized in two states: sabr in hardship and shukr in blessing. Together they cover every state of human life. Shukr has three dimensions: gratitude in the heart (acknowledging the blessing), gratitude on the tongue (saying Alhamdulillah and expressing thanks), and gratitude in action (using the blessing in Allah's service).

For corps members: your education, your posting opportunity, your health, your colleagues, your community — all are blessings from Allah. Shukr means using every one of these in His service.
wednesday.extra_notes: The opposite of shukr is kufr an-ni'mah (ingratitude for blessing) — which is not full kufr (disbelief) but is a serious sin that leads to removal of blessings. The practical test: Do you attribute your achievements to your own intelligence and hard work alone? That is the beginning of ingratitude.
wednesday.source: Tafsir Ibn Kathir, Quran 14:7; Uddat as-Sabirin wa Dhakhirat ash-Shakirin by Ibn al-Qayyim; Madarij as-Salikin by Ibn al-Qayyim

thursday.title: Fiqh of Funerals — Janazah Rites
thursday.arabic_text: أَكْثِرُوا ذِكْرَ هَاذِمِ اللَّذَّاتِ: الْمَوْتَ
thursday.english_text: Increase your remembrance of the destroyer of pleasures: death.
thursday.lesson:
The Islamic funeral rite (janazah) has specific steps: closing the eyes of the deceased, bathing (ghusl), wrapping in white shrouds (kafan), Salat al-Janazah (funeral prayer), and burial in the ground facing the Qiblah. The Salat al-Janazah is fard kifayah (collective obligation) — if some Muslims perform it, the rest are relieved of the obligation.

For a corps member who loses a colleague, community member, or relative during their service year: knowing these basic rites is a religious obligation. At minimum, know the Salat al-Janazah: four takbeers, Surah al-Fatihah after first, salawat on the Prophet after second, du'a for the deceased after third, and salam after fourth.
thursday.extra_notes:
Du'a for the deceased in Salat al-Janazah:
'Allahumma ighfir lahu warhamhu wa 'aafihee wa'fu 'anhu' — O Allah, forgive him, have mercy on him, grant him wellbeing, and pardon him. (Sahih Muslim 963)

Condolences: Say to the bereaved family: 'Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un. A'dhamalahu ajrak wa ahsana 'aza'ak wa ghafara li-mayyitik.' — To Allah we belong and to Him we return. May Allah magnify your reward, make your bereavement beautiful, and forgive your deceased.
thursday.source: Fiqh us-Sunnah by Sayyid Sabiq, Vol. 1; Al-Mughni by Ibn Qudamah; Hisn al-Muslim by Sa'id al-Qahtani

thursday.title: Fiqh of Waqf — Islamic Endowment for Community Good
thursday.arabic_text: إِذَا مَاتَ الإِنْسَانُ انْقَطَعَ عَنْهُ عَمَلُهُ إِلَّا مِنْ ثَلَاثَةٍ: إِلَّا مِنْ صَدَقَةٍ جَارِيَةٍ
thursday.english_text: When a person dies, their deeds cease except from three: ongoing charity (sadaqah jariyah)...
thursday.lesson:
Waqf (Islamic endowment) is the dedication of an asset — land, building, money, books — for ongoing community benefit in the way of Allah. The income or utility continues to benefit the community permanently, and the reward continues to flow to the donor after death.

Classic examples: Umar ibn al-Khattab's land endowment, Uthman's purchase of the well of Rumah. Modern examples: building a masjid, endowing a school library, donating medical equipment to a clinic.

For corps members: even small acts of lasting benefit count as sadaqah jariyah — teaching Quran to children, building a garden, repairing a community water point. Plant something that outlives your service year.
thursday.source: Sahih Muslim, Hadith 1631; Al-Fiqh al-Islami wa Adillatuh by Wahbah az-Zuhayli; Al-Mughni by Ibn Qudamah

friday.title: Making the Most of the Hidden Hour of Friday
friday.arabic_text: فِي يَوْمِ الْجُمُعَةِ سَاعَةٌ لَا يُوَافِقُهَا عَبْدٌ مُسْلِمٌ وَهُوَ قَائِمٌ يُصَلِّي يَسْأَلُ اللَّهَ شَيْئًا إِلَّا أَعْطَاهُ إِيَّاهُ
friday.english_text: On Friday there is a moment — no Muslim servant stands in prayer asking Allah for something at that time, except that He gives it to him.
friday.lesson:
The Sa'ah al-Mustajabah (the hour of answered du'a on Friday) is real and guaranteed by the Prophet. The two strongest scholarly opinions on its time: (1) when the imam sits between the two khutbahs (imam sits down briefly), and (2) the last hour before Maghrib on Friday. The second opinion is more widely held and more practically accessible.

Practical guide: From roughly 45 minutes before Maghrib on Friday, dedicate this time entirely to du'a. Write down your du'a in advance — for yourself, your family, your community, the Ummah. Do not waste this guaranteed window of response.
friday.extra_notes:
What to ask for in the Friday hour:
- Forgiveness of sins
- Guidance and firmness in faith
- Good spouse, righteous children
- Halal provision and freedom from debt
- Success in your service year
- Healing for the sick
- Peace for the Ummah
- Entrance into Jannah and protection from Hellfire
friday.source: Sahih al-Bukhari, Hadith 935; Sahih Muslim, Hadith 852; Riyad as-Salihin, Chapter on Friday Du'a

friday.title: Friday Azkar — Du'a for Good Character
friday.arabic_text: اللَّهُمَّ كَمَا حَسَّنْتَ خَلْقِي فَحَسِّنْ خُلُقِي
friday.english_text: O Allah, just as You have made my physical form beautiful, beautify my character.
friday.transliteration: Allahumma kama hassanta khalqi fahassin khuluqi.
friday.benefits: This du'a was made by the Prophet when looking in a mirror. It links external form — which Allah shaped at creation — to internal character, which is shaped through effort and divine guidance throughout life. For the corps member: your physical appearance is a gift already given. Your character is a gift you must ask for and work toward. Make this du'a on Friday and every day when you look in a mirror.
friday.source: Musnad Ahmad, Hadith 3823; Authenticated by al-Albani in Silsilah as-Sahihah (1307); Hisn al-Muslim by Sa'id al-Qahtani

saturday.title: Muadh ibn Jabal (RA) — The Scholar of Halal and Haram
saturday.arabic_text: أَعْلَمُ أُمَّتِي بِالْحَلَالِ وَالْحَرَامِ مُعَاذُ بْنُ جَبَلٍ
saturday.english_text: The most knowledgeable of my Ummah regarding halal and haram is Muadh ibn Jabal.
saturday.lesson:
Muadh ibn Jabal (RA) was appointed by the Prophet as the governor and teacher of Yemen — at just 22 years of age. When the Prophet sent him, he gave him this famous guidance: 'What will you judge by?' Muadh said: 'The Book of Allah.' The Prophet asked: 'And if you don't find it there?' Muadh said: 'The Sunnah of the Prophet.' The Prophet asked: 'And if not there?' Muadh said: 'I will make my own reasoned judgment (ijtihad).' The Prophet was pleased.

Muadh died in the plague of Amwas in 18 AH at just 34 years old — yet his knowledge and decisions shaped Islamic jurisprudence permanently.

Lesson: Young age does not disqualify you from significant responsibility if you have knowledge, sincerity, and the right methodology.
saturday.source: Jami' al-Tirmidhi, Hadith 3790; Sunan Abi Dawud, Hadith 3592; Siyar A'lam an-Nubala by Imam adh-Dhahabi

saturday.title: Umm Waraqah bint Abdillah (RA) — The Quran Memorizer
saturday.arabic_text: كَانَتِ النَّبِيُّ يَزُورُهَا فِي بَيْتِهَا وَجَعَلَ لَهَا مُؤَذِّنًا
saturday.english_text: The Prophet would visit her in her home and appointed a muadhdhin for her.
saturday.lesson:
Umm Waraqah bint Abdillah al-Ansariyyah (RA) had memorized the entire Quran — a distinction that earned her the Prophet's personal visits to her home. She asked permission to participate in the Battle of Badr to tend the wounded and shroud the martyrs. The Prophet gave her the title 'the Martyr' (ash-shaheedah) during her lifetime, foretelling her fate.
